case_facts.question: What is the current state of geothermal energy in Europe: installed electricity capacity, recent growth, and the policy direction?
case_facts.output: Markdown report; key findings first; every figure in a table with source and date
case_facts.conflict_policy: two sources disagree on a figure -> show both with dates; never pick one, never average

findings.claim: Installed geothermal electricity capacity in Europe reached 3.5 GW at the end of 2022 across 142 operating plants, with growth concentrated in Türkiye, Italy and Iceland.
findings.title: European Geothermal Council — Geothermal Market Report 2022
findings.excerpt: Installed geothermal electricity capacity in Europe reached 3.5 GW at the end of 2022, with 142 plants in operation. Growth was concentrated in Türkiye, Italy and Iceland.

findings.claim: Europe's geothermal power capacity stood at 4.0 GW at end-2024, up 4% year on year, and remains under 1% of the region's renewable electricity capacity.
findings.title: Global Renewables Statistics Agency — Renewable Capacity Statistics 2025
findings.excerpt: Europe's geothermal power capacity stood at 4.0 GW at end-2024, up 4% year on year. Geothermal remains under 1% of the region's renewable electricity capacity.

findings.claim: A 12-country European review found the median time from exploration licence to plant commissioning was 6.5 years, identifying permitting rather than resource risk as the binding constraint on geothermal policy.
findings.title: Permitting bottlenecks for geothermal power in Europe: a 12-country review
findings.excerpt: Across twelve European countries the median time from exploration licence to plant commissioning was 6.5 years; permitting, not resource risk, was the binding constraint on geothermal policy.

findings.claim: Geothermal district heating in Europe reached 412 systems in operation at the end of 2023, with a further 300 projects under development, with France, Germany and the Netherlands accounting for most new capacity.
findings.title: European Geothermal Council — Geothermal Heating and Cooling Outlook 2024
findings.excerpt: Geothermal district heating in Europe reached 412 systems in operation at the end of 2023, with a further 300 projects under development. France, Germany and the Netherlands account for most new capacity.

findings.claim: The outlook projects that geothermal district heating could supply 25% of Europe's heat demand by 2040 if drilling costs fall by a third.
findings.title: European Geothermal Council — Geothermal Heating and Cooling Outlook 2024
findings.excerpt: The outlook estimates that district heating could supply 25% of Europe's heat demand by 2040 if drilling costs fall by a third.

findings.claim: On policy context, survey respondents rank permitting time as the top market barrier, geological risk second and access to capital third, and only six countries operate a public risk-insurance scheme.
findings.title: European Geothermal Council — Geothermal Heating and Cooling Outlook 2024
findings.excerpt: Respondents in the council's survey rank permitting time first and geological risk second; access to capital ranks third. Only six countries operate a public risk-insurance scheme.

findings.claim: A 12-country European review found the median time from exploration licence to geothermal plant commissioning was 6.5 years, identifying permitting rather than resource risk as the binding policy constraint.
findings.title: Permitting bottlenecks for geothermal power in Europe: a 12-country review
findings.excerpt: Across twelve European countries the median time from exploration licence to plant commissioning was 6.5 years; permitting, not resource risk, was the binding constraint on geothermal policy.

findings.claim: Public geological risk insurance schemes in four European countries increased the share of exploratory geothermal wells drilled by non-utility developers from 12% to 31% within five years.
findings.title: Geological risk insurance schemes as geothermal policy instruments in Europe
findings.excerpt: Public geological risk insurance in four European countries raised the share of exploratory wells drilled by non-utility developers from 12% to 31% within five years.
